lesson.title: The Y-Intercept: A Line's Starting Height
lesson.summary: The y-intercept is the point where a line's graph crosses the vertical axis, found by setting x equal to zero, and it appears directly as the constant term in slope-intercept form.
lesson.body:
Just as every point on the horizontal axis has a y-coordinate of zero, every point on the vertical axis has an x-coordinate of zero. The y-intercept of a line is the point where that line's graph crosses the vertical axis, meaning it is the one point on the line where x = 0. Finding it algebraically works the same way as finding the x-intercept, just with the roles of x and y reversed: substitute x = 0 into the equation of the line and solve for y. Unlike the x-intercept, a non-vertical line always has exactly one y-intercept, since every valid function assigns exactly one output to the input x = 0, and there is only one input value equal to zero to plug in.

Here is a worked example using the same line from the previous two chapters, y = 3x - 2. Set x equal to 0: y = 3(0) - 2 = 0 - 2 = -2. So the y-intercept is the point (0, -2). This is not a new calculation from scratch; it matches exactly the first point calculated back when the linear function chapter evaluated f(0), which also came out to -2. That consistency is expected, since evaluating a function at x = 0 and finding its y-intercept are the same operation viewed from two different chapters, just described with different vocabulary.

This connection reveals something worth noticing about the form y = mx + b, called slope-intercept form. The constant term b is always the y-intercept, with no calculation required at all. In the equation y = 3x - 2, the constant term is -2, matching the y-intercept (0, -2) found by direct substitution. This is because setting x = 0 makes the mx term disappear entirely, since m times 0 is 0, leaving only y = b. Recognizing an equation written in this form lets you read off the y-intercept instantly, without solving anything, which makes slope-intercept form especially convenient for quick graphing.

The y-intercept also has a natural real-world reading in many applied problems: it represents the starting value before any input is applied, such as an initial fee before usage charges, or a starting height before any change over time. In y = 3x - 2, if x represented time and y represented some quantity, the y-intercept of -2 would represent the value of that quantity at the very start, when time equals zero, before any of the rate of change described by the slope has had a chance to act. A negative starting value like this is common in applied settings too, such as a bank account that begins in debt before deposits bring it upward over time.

Together, the x-intercept and y-intercept give two guaranteed points on any non-horizontal, non-vertical line, which is often enough to sketch its entire graph by hand: plot both intercepts, then draw a single straight line connecting them, exactly as described in the graph of a line chapter, without needing to calculate any further points at all.
